studies.title: The Best Proportion, The Lowest Fall
studies.meaning: Three oaths and a geography. Scholars read the fig and the olive as places or as fruits, and the sources record both without deciding; the mountain and the city are Sinai and Mecca. Then the claim and its reversal in two lines. The human being was made in the finest proportion and then returned to the lowest of the low. Commentators differ over what the return is: old age, or moral collapse, or the fire.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and early. The three places named have been read as a sequence of revelations: the land where earlier prophets were sent, the mountain where Moses received the law, and the city where the final message began. That reading is old and widely repeated, though the sources also record the simpler view that the first two are fruits. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From the root for standing straight and for setting something right. It covers physical uprightness and correct arrangement together, so the phrase means both well-made and standing.
A superlative doubled with its own plural, a construction that pushes the meaning as far down as Arabic will go. Nothing is named as the destination, only a direction and its extreme.
From the root for safety and for trust, the same root behind the word for a believer and the title given to a reliable man. Applied to a city it names a place where a person is not attacked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Figs and olives did not grow in Mecca. They came from the north, from the hills of Syria and Palestine, and arrived as trade goods with a season and a price. Naming them at the head of a surah pointed a Meccan listener up the caravan road toward country he had heard about all his life, and the mountain named next lay along the same route.
studies.didYouKnow: A companion is reported to have said that he never heard a finer voice or recitation than the Prophet's when he recited this surah in an evening prayer on a journey. The report is preserved in the major collections. The surah is eight ayat long, and its rhyme runs on a single syllable from the first line to the last.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two statements about the human being are set beside each other without either being withdrawn. The best proportion is asserted, and then the lowest position, and the surah does not explain how both are true of the same creature. That refusal is the passage's honesty: it names the height and the fall as facts of the same nature, and the exemption that follows in the next ayah is granted to conduct rather than to species.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the exemption this passage sets up, granted for conduct rather than for being human.
Describes the same making with four verbs, and attaches a question about ingratitude to it.
States the high estimate on its own, without the fall placed immediately beside it.

studies.applyIt: Hold both halves of this surah about one person you find difficult. Made in the best proportion; capable of the lowest. Not one or the other. Most disagreements run on picking a half and staying there, and this passage refuses to, which is harder and more accurate than either option on its own.

studies.title: A Reward Without End
studies.meaning: An exception is hung on a bleak statement, and it rescues by category rather than by name: those who believed and did the works. Their reward is then described by a denial. The word ruled out carries two senses at once, severing and reproaching, so the reward is both uninterrupted and free of anyone holding it over them. Two questions close the surah and neither is answered. The first asks what still makes the hearer deny the reckoning; the second asks whether God is not the best of judges.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The oaths that open the surah name places long associated with earlier prophecy and then the city the audience was standing in, so the argument is set inside a geography of revelation before it says anything. Classical sources report no occasion for these closing lines and read the questions as addressed to a single listener rather than to the opposition as a body.

keyTerms.gloss: cut off, or held over one
keyTerms.note: The root joins severing something and reminding a person of a favour until it weighs on him. Denying both at once makes the reward continuous and also free of any obligation attached to it.
One word covers a debt, a recompense and a religion, all from the sense of what is owed and then settled. Here the commentators read the accounting rather than the creed.
A superlative from a root meaning both to judge and to make something firm, so the best judge is also the one whose ruling holds. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Mecca went to arbitration, and an arbitrator's ruling had no force behind it beyond his reputation. A powerful clan could simply decline. Compensation for a killing was negotiated rather than imposed, and the settlement depended on who could be pressured. Everyone hearing the last line had watched a judgement ignored by someone strong enough to ignore it, which is what gives the question its edge.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming God as the most just of judges occurs in only one other place in the Quran, where it is spoken by Noah as he appeals over the loss of his own son. The same four words serve as the close of a public argument here and as the last resort of a grieving father there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception clause is the structural centre of the surah, and it is worth noticing how little it demands: belief and work, described in general terms, with no quantity attached. Everything before it has been about descent from a high origin, and this one clause interrupts that descent without reversing the account of it. Then the closing questions hand the argument to the hearer instead of finishing it for him.

crossReferences.why: Contains the only other use of the phrase about the best of judges, in Noah's appeal to his Lord.
Ends another short surah with the identical promise of a reward that is never cut off.
Uses the same exception clause to rescue humanity from a blanket statement of loss.

studies.applyIt: Answer the surah's question out loud in one sentence, as though it had been put to you personally, because it has. Not what people in general say, and not a defence of anyone else. What, after all this, still makes you treat the reckoning as unreal. Say it once and then leave it alone.
